claim: A coin shortage explains why one Dutch city hands out free herring.

start.title: Coin
start.description: Small, flat and usually round piece of material used as money

knots.passage: The first attested siege coins appeared at the siege of Pavia in 1524.
knots.hatnote: When a city is surrounded, soldiers still want paying. So it makes its own money.

knots.passage: During the Eighty Years' War a number of towns and cities issued their own currency (money of necessity), for example during the siege of Leiden (1573–1574), the authorities issued diamond (square) silver coinage struck with a circular die. When silver ran out they used the same die to print money on cardboard. This was the first usage of paper money in Europe.
knots.hatnote: In one besieged Dutch town, even the silver ran out.

knots.section: Second siege and relief of Leiden
knots.passage: This was a formidable obstacle, but the Spaniards, adept at land fighting and not amphibious warfare, had despaired of maintaining so unequal a contest against the combined forces of the sea and the veteran Dutch seamen. Accordingly, the Spanish commander Valdez ordered a retreat in the night of 2 October, and the army fled, rendered more fearful by a terrible crash they heard from the city, and assumed to be the men of Leiden breaking still another dam upon them. In fact, part of the wall of Leiden, eroded by the sea water, had fallen, leaving the city completely vulnerable to attack, had any Spaniards chosen to remain.
knots.hatnote: Rebels flooded the land to rescue Leiden. In October 1574, the water finally rose.

knots.passage: The 3 October Festival is celebrated every year in Leiden. It is a festival, with a funfair and a dozen open air discos in the night. The municipality gives free herring and white bread to the citizens of Leiden.
knots.hatnote: Leiden has never forgotten its rescue.

knots.passage: William and his soldiers sailed to Leiden as part of a makeshift military fleet dubbed the Watergeuzen ("Sea Beggars") on the morning of 3 October. They headed north along the Vliet canal, which now had water deep enough to support their boats, and brought food and other supplies to Leiden's citizens. The food supplies primarily consisted of herring and white bread (haring en wittebrood). To reward the city's citizens for withstanding the Spanish attack, William established Leiden University the following year.
knots.hatnote: Why herring? Look at what the rescuers carried in on 3 October 1574.

payoff: Leiden ran so short of silver it printed cardboard money; it survived, won a university, and still hands out the rescuers' herring every 3 October.
caveats: 'First usage of paper money in Europe' is the Siege money page's claim; other pages credit later issuers such as Stockholm's banknotes, and this is debated.
